tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Case Study: One Play and Aaron Donald Under Expected Points Saved

**What it is** — Two worked examples from Ben Jenkins's talk.

**The 6-yard-loss play.** A running play where the ball carrier is tackled behind the line for a 6-yard loss (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). Traditional metrics credit only the tackler (JHgeEo3n1do [00:31]). Under the speaker's model the tackler has the highest value, and "four other players" also contribute positively. The speaker reads this as the model capturing coordinated effort and identifying "setup players who are largely invisible in traditional metrics" (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The captions do not show the values.

**Aaron Donald.** The speaker compares the distribution of EPA when Donald makes a tackle with the distribution when he does not, and takes the difference as his expected points saved. The captions describe the orange and blue distributions inconsistently, so which is tackle and which is no tackle is unclear (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40]). His EPS "is around 0.27, meaning each Donald tackle prevents around 0.27 expected points for the offense" (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40], [07:09]). In Q&A he says Donald in the backfield who forces the ball carrier elsewhere gets positive credit, and on a pass play he can reduce the odds the pass is beneficial (JHgeEo3n1do [11:13]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's interpretation is that the tackle effect is the gap between the two EPA distributions (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40]). The talk offers no independent confirmation that 0.27 is correct. Inference: with no known true effect (the speaker notes real causal effects are not observable, JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]), a single player's number is a model output, not a measured fact.

**When to apply** — Use as a template for reading a per-player "value per event" figure: ask what the event is, what the comparison is, and what the distributions look like before reading the difference. Inference: for Baylor, a per-event figure from any vendor deserves the same questions.

**When NOT to apply** — These are single examples (one play, one player) from a proof-of-concept run on the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). `untested`. The Donald figure is for an NFL defensive tackle on NFL tracking data and has no meaning for another level of play. The Q&A answer on pass plays and disruption without a tackle is general, and the captions give no values (JHgeEo3n1do [11:13]).

**Example** — The speaker's, above.

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], [[claim--defender-interference-in-68-percent-of-plays]].

# CLIP Is Said to Beat Other Methods at Finding Top Linemen and Ranking by Salary

**What it is** — Jenkins reports three external comparisons (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [06:33], [07:03], [07:34]):

1. The causal model was "significantly better" at identifying top offensive linemen as indicated by All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors, shown as dark green shading in a chart.
2. It was "significantly better" in ranking players by salary, "much more consistent".
3. Aggregated on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, there is a "strong positive correlation" with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences he attributes to PFF having the entire data set while his team had the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 season (caption "2020 2021").

He adds that the model correlates strongly with completion percentage on individual plays, so teams with better lines complete more passes and win more games over a season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no numbers: "significantly" has no test statistic, no correlation coefficient and no sample size in the talk. Inference: agreement with honors, salary and PFF shows the metric resembles consensus judgment, which is not evidence that the credit is causal.

**When to apply** — As an example of what external validation a vendor presents. Ask for the correlation values, the sample, what happens when honors and salary are held out, and whether the model finds linemen the consensus misses (the question that matters for recruiting, Inference).

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Eric-authored SportSmith, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: a method that mostly reproduces PFF rankings adds cost without new insight unless it disagrees with them usefully, and the talk does not show that.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no numbers back "significantly better", and honors and salary are shaped by the same reputation the model is compared with. The sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. The speaker is from the company that built the method. Do not use this entry to claim CLIP is more accurate than PFF grades.

**Example** — The comparison with PFF rankings on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, differing partly because PFF had the full season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:03]).

# About half of the familiarity gain is shot selection and half is accuracy

**What it is** — The speakers report that the accuracy curve (actual minus expected points) has nearly the same shape as the shot-selection curve, with about 7% improvement after 50 shots and gradual gain afterward, and a partial reset next season (o4rMbhsdk0I [12:18], [12:49]). Over the first 50 shots, they say each accounts for roughly half of the overall improvement: "about 50% of the gain is just that shot quality and then the other 50% is the accuracy" (o4rMbhsdk0I [15:54]). The 7% line at [16:26] is garbled in the captions ("a 7% field goal percentage"), so the unit of the accuracy gain is not clear.

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism that the model tests. The speaker, a former coach, offers explanations that are not in the model: confidence ("your brain doesn't get in the way"), rhythm and timing, and passer-specific preferences for pass placement (chest-high, a lower shooting pocket, left or right) (o4rMbhsdk0I [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]). The speaker says "we don't know because it's not in the model" (o4rMbhsdk0I [13:52]). In the Q&A the speakers say the accuracy piece cannot be separated into better off-ball screening versus better passing with current data (o4rMbhsdk0I [40:33], [41:03]). Inference: confidence and rhythm are hypotheses until measured.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to split any "got better together" result into what was chosen and what was executed before acting on it. Inference: a unit that improves because it picks better opportunities needs a different response (play design, spacing) from one that executes better (reps, timing).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested because the 50/50 split rests on one model and a slide, with no uncertainty shown, and the accuracy side depends on an assumed 1.2 expected-points baseline (o4rMbhsdk0I [12:18]). The speakers call their numbers rule of thumb (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]). Do not read the split as exact or as portable to other sports or play types. The coaching explanations are one speaker's view, not findings.

**Example** — The talk's own illustration is the Phoenix trio (see [[case-study--phoenix-suns-chris-paul-familiarity-ramp]]).

**Related** — [[claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality]], [[framework--familiarity-counter-log-log-shot-quality-model]].

# Kentucky's Linemen Averaged 1.54 Load per Contact in Their Hardest Practice Against 2.22 in Games

**What it is** — Morris compared practice to game using the line metric. His reported figures:
- Average game load per contact 2.22; on the most intense practice day (Tuesday) 1.54 (QLdbKUiNadg [08:16], [08:47]).
- The practice week was supposed to peak on Tuesday, and distance was fine, but contact and load per contact were not (QLdbKUiNadg [08:16], [08:47]).
- Only first-team offense against first-team defense, and one-on-ones, came near game intensity; team versus scout team gave the most contact load, but scout players "don't go nearly as hard" (QLdbKUiNadg [09:18], [09:48]).
- About 3.5 game-like reps in one period and 1.5 in another, "about five game reps in a practice" (QLdbKUiNadg [09:48]).
- In games, contacts account for about 66% of total player load (the caption says "a hundred sixty-six percent" and then "sixty six percent", read here as 66%, QLdbKUiNadg [10:19]).
- "By the time we get to the game we increase our contact load by over a hundred percent" (QLdbKUiNadg [10:19]).

=== claim--post-ucl-surgery-return-rate-and-performance-studies-disagree.md
---

# After UCL ("Tommy John") surgery, about 80% return, but whether performance rises is disputed

**What it is** — Glenn Fleisig (title spelling; caption "fleig") of the American Sports Medicine Institute (ASMI) reviews what happens to pitchers after ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (AgouMNTeyo4 [06:08]).

Return and time:
- Three studies in the same journal, on largely the same pitchers, tracked how pitchers did afterward: one covering 1974 to 2012, one of 147 pitchers since 1999, one of the 38 most recent pitchers with PitchFX data since 2008 (caption names "Ericson", "mcne", "Jang"; spellings unverified) (AgouMNTeyo4 [20:04], [20:35], [21:05]).
- About 80% of major leaguers return, 20% do not; in the middle study 80% made it back for at least one game but only about 67% "made it back and stayed there" (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:10], [22:40]).
- Published studies put the return to the majors at about a year and a half; ASMI's own data (Dr Andrews' patients, major league, minor league or amateur) show about 80% return in about 12 months, and he explains the gap as waiting for the next season (AgouMNTeyo4 [22:40], [24:15]).
- Age at surgery does not change the roughly 80% chance of returning to the same level or higher (high school, college, pro), but for a 16 year old "we don't have enough long-term data" and he calls it "a worrisome road" (AgouMNTeyo4 [56:34], [57:05]).

Performance: the first study said pitchers got better after surgery; the other two did not, finding performance "down like controls", that is, as an age-matched decline would predict. Fleisig says "I kind of believe" the second and third (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:05], [21:39], [22:10]). He adds that his own group's pitchers' stats "went down like the controls" (AgouMNTeyo4 [23:43]).

Definitions of success: the cited studies used at least 10 major league games; Fleisig says he would define success as staying healthy (off the disabled list, no repeat surgery) and statistics that match the age group (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02], [54:32]).

**Why it works** — Fleisig's explanation for the performance disagreement is age: pitchers having surgery at 30 or 33 would naturally decline, so comparing to the pre-surgery self overstates the change (AgouMNTeyo4 [21:39]). Inference: the three studies differ in who is counted and in what the comparator is, which is why a trajectory matched to age or role is the better yardstick.

**When to apply** — When defining what "back" means for an athlete returning from a major surgery: define it by several criteria, set the comparison to an age- and role-expected path, and state the time window before anyone judges the return.

Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports return-to-performance decisions with information (Explicit, Playbook p.6), contributes "Testing and progression" with shared loading decisions, and the involvement "doesn't really end" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4, Q4a). A written protocol exists in the UE and LE rehab templates, but Flint has not read them. Inference: Fleisig's multi-part success definition could be set against those templates once staged; the baseline does not hold return criteria.

**When NOT to apply** — Elbow reconstruction in baseball pitchers only; do not transfer the 80%, 67% or 12 to 18 month figures to football or to other injuries. The 16% prevalence and 25% major league figures and the ASMI return data come from a study he says is unpublished or from his own center (AgouMNTeyo4 [08:13], [23:11]). The three-study summary has garbled author names, and the speaker says he is not a medical doctor (AgouMNTeyo4 [19:33]). The first study disagrees with the other two on performance; the 2017 speaker says the medical research shows no performance gain, which sides with the latter two (sHXuxj3-rbQ [06:17]), and reports that, preliminarily, players with a second surgery came back less strongly (sHXuxj3-rbQ [04:12]). The 10-game bar may be low for a star pitcher.

**Example** — The speaker's own, from the Q&A: asked how to define success for two high-profile returning pitchers, he said the studies' bar was at least 10 major league games, that some injured pitchers were marginal major leaguers to begin with, which makes that a reasonable criterion for them, and that he would define success as staying healthy and statistics matching the age group (AgouMNTeyo4 [53:32], [54:02], [54:32]).

**Related** — [[claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents]] (what players expect the surgery to do, from a 2017 talk that cites a survey also shown here at [18:30]); [[framework--prospective-baseline-then-follow-cohort-from-the-draft]]; [[principle--competitive-exposure-required-before-return-to-play]] (Harries).
=== claim--sleep-extension-improved-stanford-athlete-performance.md
---

# Extending Time in Bed to Ten Hours for Six Weeks Improved Stanford Athletes' Performance

**What it is** — The speaker (a sleep scientist, unnamed) summarizes the Stanford sleep-extension studies: athletes were given 10 hours in bed for six weeks, wore actigraphs, kept sleep diaries, and were tested near the end of the six weeks (J7smyg1Czik [09:12], [09:42]). Reported results: basketball players had a significant reduction in sprint times and a 9% increase in both free throws and three-point field goals, were less sleepy, and rated their mood better (J7smyg1Czik [09:42], [10:13]); football players shaved time off the 40-yard dash and the 20-yard shuttle (the caption reads "1 point1 2 seconds", garbled, so the amount is not confirmed) (J7smyg1Czik [10:13], [10:44]); swimmers improved average turn time and added "five kicks" to their strokes (caption wording, unclear) (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]); tennis players improved serve accuracy (J7smyg1Czik [11:14]). From these she says adults need 7 to 8 hours but athletes need 9 to 10 (J7smyg1Czik [08:42], [09:12], [11:14]). The 9 to 10 hour figure is her synthesis of these studies, not a stated finding of any one of them. In the Q&A she acknowledges the extension studies measured time in bed, not sleep (J7smyg1Czik [25:57]).

**Why it works** — The speaker connects the gains to the effects listed earlier in her talk (reaction time, judgment, mood) but gives no direct mechanism for these results. Inference: the improvements may come from reduced chronic sleep loss in athletes who started short, not from sleeping more than needed; the talk does not report baseline sleep.

**When to apply** — As background when an athlete group is plainly short on sleep and the schedule allows more time in bed (for example, no early-morning facility constraints). Inference: this supports aiming to enable more time in bed before aiming at a specific hour target. Eric's baseline: sleep is not tracked and recovery is managed through training-load design alone (interview 2026-09-28, Q23, Explicit). The speaker also says sports limited by facility times, such as swimming and ice hockey, are hit hardest (J7smyg1Czik [23:55]).

**When NOT to apply** — Sample sizes, effect sizes (beyond the 9% shooting figures) and statistics are not given, and no control group is described in the talk. Time in bed was extended, so quality and total sleep were not measured. The athletes are Stanford athletes in four sports; there is no football-position, no NFL and no Baylor data. The 9 to 10 hours target should not be read as a requirement: the speaker says individual need varies in the Q&A (J7smyg1Czik [26:58]). A 2017 conference talk with no stated citation for the studies.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Stanford basketball players with a 9% increase in free throws and in three-point field goals after six weeks of 10 hours in bed (J7smyg1Czik [09:42]).

**Related** — [[claim--sleep-debt-accumulates-and-three-recovery-nights-do-not-erase-it]]; [[heuristic--weekend-sleep-extension-signals-a-deficit]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/lever-2024-a-preliminary-investigation-of-the-relationship-between-sleep-and-nap-behavior-of-ncaa-div]]; [[research-papers/vitale-2026-from-gpt-4-to-expert-endorsed-athlete-guidance-a-delphi-consensus-on-sleep-and-jet-lag]].
=== claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery.md
---

# Year-Round Youth Baseball: Arm Pain Is Common, Pressure to Play On Is Common

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally gives early single-sport specialization and year-round play as the second reason UCL surgeries are not falling (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]). He says specialization before kids are skeletally mature is "causing a burnout" of muscles and tendons (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]).

- **Survey:** 200 healthy youth baseball players who were not complaining of pain, surveyed "when I was in residency in New York City." 75% admitted arm pain (z_6M5r7031A [07:10]). 25% had symptoms suggestive of a legitimate overuse injury, and 50% felt pressured to play despite admitting arm pain, by coaches and parents (z_6M5r7031A [07:41]).
- **Draft:** a Mayo Clinic study by Chris Camp (caption spelling), which the speaker reports second-hand, found up to 10% of drafted pitchers, high school and college, had already had Tommy John surgery, at an increasing rate year by year (z_6M5r7031A [07:41] to [08:11]).
- **Youngest case:** the youngest he has operated on was 12 (z_6M5r7031A [08:11]).
- **Qualifier (Q&A):** some early throwing is necessary because the arm remodels in childhood, including the humerus, so a child who never threw cannot take up pitching at 12; "the challenge is giving some rest" (z_6M5r7031A [19:51] to [20:21]). Pitch counts are undermined when school and travel leagues each count separately, and 15 warm-up pitches between innings add to a 70-pitch count (z_6M5r7031A [20:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated cause is no rest for the shoulder and elbow muscles across fall, winter, spring, summer, travel and high school ball (z_6M5r7031A [06:40]). The survey shows prevalence of pain and perceived pressure; it does not by itself show that specialization caused the injuries. Inference: the survey is cross-sectional, so cause cannot be read from it.

**When to apply** — As an outside prompt when Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance take medical or injury history from incoming baseball or softball athletes. Inference: ask about prior surgery and year-round throwing history, since the draft figure suggests earlier overuse changes what a prospect brings. Eric's baseline: progressions in volume and intensity are kept smooth, and abrupt changes are treated as an injury-risk driver (Inferred, HHPR 5355 course team position, speaker unconfirmed). Inference: this talk extends that with a youth-sport mechanism, accumulated load with no rest, which the baseline does not cover.

**When NOT to apply** — The survey's sample source, selection method and ages are not given beyond "200 healthy youth baseball players" in one residency setting. Self-reported pain is not a diagnosis. The Mayo figure is "up to 10%" and second-hand. The talk does not show that specialization causes the burnout; that is the speaker's assertion. Baseball pitching only. Not evidence about college or football athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: Little League kids icing their elbows after games, and facilities in Michigan full of children playing indoors in snow (z_6M5r7031A [06:10] to [07:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more]] (the first cause the speaker gives). [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (what happens after surgery).
=== framework--expected-value-decision-analysis-for-treatment-choice.md
---

# Expected Value Decision Analysis for Surgery Versus Non-Operative Care

**What it is** — Dr. Eric McNally proposes expected value decision analysis as "an adjunct to our clinical care" for a UCL injury, after saying his group has used it in other parts of orthopedic surgery (z_6M5r7031A [15:46], [17:49]). The structure he describes:
1. **Two branches:** surgery, or non-operative treatment (the "top wing" and "bottom wing," z_6M5r7031A [16:16] to [16:47]).
2. **One outcome to maximize:** pitcher wins above replacement (WAR) in his example (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).
3. **Inputs, known and unknown:** the likelihood of healing with and without surgery, the likely performance on return, and when the injury happened (z_6M5r7031A [15:46] to [16:16]). Context changes the answer: spring training versus a few months before the playoffs, and an ace on a team with no playoff chance versus a team on the bubble (z_6M5r7031A [16:16]).
4. **Output:** an expected value per branch. In his sample model, one representative scenario, expected WAR was 1.6 non-operative versus 1.3 with surgery (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).
5. **Two-way sensitivity analysis:** a grid where blue tiles show surgery producing a better WAR and green tiles show non-operative care doing so, with threshold values for success by treatment based on clinical characteristics, prior attempts and tear characteristics. It lets the user toggle unknown inputs (z_6M5r7031A [17:19] to [17:49]).

Inputs he cites elsewhere: non-operative success of 40 to 80% depending on the case with at most a 3-month downtime, and surgery success of "80 to 100%" in different studies (caption "80 to 80 to 100%," garbled) with a year to a year and a half of downtime (z_6M5r7031A [14:14] to [14:45]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no argument beyond saying the model lets you "optimize for any outcome you want" and test unknown inputs (z_6M5r7031A [16:16], [17:49]). Inference: its value is making the assumptions explicit and showing where a decision flips, not producing a verdict.

**When to apply** — As an illustration when explaining a try-conservative-care versus choose-surgery conversation to coaches. Eric's baseline: Applied Performance's stated role is to supply information that supports Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions (Explicit, Playbook p.6), and what it contributes in return to performance is testing and progression with shared loading decisions (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q4). Eric's baseline: "We don't assess readiness. The template answers that" (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q22). Inference: a decision tree is a communication aid within that supporting role, and the probabilities in it belong to Athletic Medicine.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the only output shown is one sample case with chosen inputs, and no validation of the model against outcomes is shown. The speaker says it "does not take the place of clinical decision-making" (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]). The objective, WAR, is a professional baseball value measure with no college equivalent. The probabilities of healing are ranges from "different studies," not Baylor data. Do not use it to pick treatment for an athlete.

**Example** — The speaker's own sample: for one representative player, expected WAR of 1.6 with non-operative care versus 1.3 with surgery, so "maybe non-operative treatment might work" for this case (z_6M5r7031A [16:47]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--price-the-failure-branch-of-conservative-care]] (the logic of why the non-operative branch needs a failure term). [[claim--ucl-reconstruction-return-outcomes-mlb-pitchers]] (data that would fill the surgery branch). Reciprocal-link suggestions: [[yung-2022-a-framework-for-clinicians-to-improve-the-decision-making-process-in-return-to-sport]] (not compared in this batch) and [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

15:The speaker, a sleep scientist who says she works with athletes and teams (and refers to a lab at Henry Ford), argues that sleep and circadian rhythm are the most ignored performance factor and touch every other one. She presents three things: why sleep matters (reaction time, judgment, injury, hormones, pain, glucose), how much athletes need (9 to 10 hours, based on extension studies), and how the body clock affects performance (travel across time zones, evening games, and individual chronotype). Her take-home points are that deficits accumulate, that regular sleep matters more than sleep before a game, and that circadian timing is an unexplored, manageable advantage. A long Q&A covers quality, individual need, naps and clock shifting.

=== framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels.md
---

# Pressure Score: A Blocker-Interference Feature and a Forgiving Label

**What it is** — Stage 3 of Hong's pipeline (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]) models pressure as a probability that a rusher gets a hit, hurry or sack, on a 0 to 1 scale "at any point in time during the play" (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:47], [09:19]). Two design choices are the useful part.

**1. A blocker-interference feature.** For each rusher, an "area of interest" is set by distance and angle between the rusher and the passer, and the number of blockers inside it is counted, to measure the resistance the rusher may meet (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [10:23]). It sits alongside the static and dynamic tracking features from the matchup stage and relative position, velocity and acceleration to the passer (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [23:43]).

**2. A forgiving target.** Targets are the manually labeled PFF hurry, hit and sack, plus an engineered label based on the rusher's distance to the passer at a point in time (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:23], [10:54]). In Q&A he describes it as one rusher getting within one yard of the passer before one second; the captions are garbled, so the exact rule is uncertain (1nt8hK2oYrE [20:39]). The reason he gives: "it is not always the one player gets a sack", so a rusher who gets into the threshold area earns credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]).

Main drivers he gives (a light feature analysis, no values stated): the rusher's relative position to the passer, velocity and acceleration, initial position (who starts close), and how many blockers the rusher faces, with an open rusher more likely to generate pressure (1nt8hK2oYrE [17:37], [18:08], [18:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the intent (credit more than the sack-taker) but no test of the engineered label. Inference: a distance-based label turns a rare event (sack) into a more frequent one, which gives a model more signal to learn from.

**When to apply** — When an event label is rare and a process variable (distance, time) is available: consider a second, softer label, and disclose how it was set. Count obstructions between a mover and a target as a feature when tracking is available.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Eric-authored, Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: label consistency is the weakest point here; PFF hurry and hit labels are subjective hand labels, and the engineered label rule is not fully stated in the talk.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no accuracy figure, no feature weights, no validation of the engineered label. The model "didn't actively account for" complex position features (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]), and team scheme and strategies are left as future work (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). It was trained on NFL data and PFF labels. The speaker did not check correlation with quarterback motion (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a passer forced out of the pocket after heavy pressure, where the model credits two rushers (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:04]).

**Related** — [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]; [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]].
=== framework--wearable-validation-workflow.md

# A Wearable Validation Workflow: Question, Prepare, Validate, Reproduce, Then Share

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") lays out a decision flow for using wearable data in research (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [34:22]):
1. **Start with the research question.** Are the data appropriate for it, and is it a high-impact question? If not, "back to the drawing board" (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19]).
2. **Prepare the data:** address sensor accuracy, missing data and outliers (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [33:51]).
3. **Validate** the wearable against something you can trust, in her example hormone measures, using a survey that gives baseline information about the wearer and a diverse group of users (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [33:51]).
4. **Reproduce known values or trends.** If not, look again. If yes, analyze (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:51]).
5. **Check for robust conclusions** that answer the question. If yes, share. If not, you learn what is missing and can refine the question and the prospective data collection (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:51] to [34:22]).

Her wider advice: use multiple wearables, validate against hormones, tweak the wearable, and ask questions over time (an7u-tVP5Xc [34:22]). Run it as a team: an endocrinologist, a sports physician, athlete input and a data analytics expert (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:14], [34:53] to [35:24]).

Background reasons she gives: sensors differ in what they measure and in validity, so "any wearable" data are "apples and oranges"; with no test against a gold standard "we're making a lot of assumptions" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:32], [28:44] to [29:14]). She also raises data quality, health equity, algorithm bias, privacy and AI repeating errors with more confidence (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:44] to [31:17]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is the validity point above: unvalidated devices carry unexamined assumptions. She gives no study showing the workflow itself improves results. Inference: the loop of step 5 treats a failed validation as information, not a wasted study.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a one-page checklist before adopting any consumer wearable, sleep or cycle-tracking product with a women's team, asking whether the device was validated against a trusted standard and in athletes like Baylor's. Eric's baseline: modified reactive strength index from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-19). Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20). Inference: the talk agrees with preferring validated, consistent measures and adds a validation step before adoption.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's flow, shown without a worked example or outcomes. Her reference standard is hormone testing for cycle-related wearables; other devices need their own trusted reference. It is a research workflow, not a procurement standard, and it does not say how much validation is enough. Her view that a team is needed is an institutional opinion; she leads an institute with philanthropic funding (an7u-tVP5Xc [25:40]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says "just plug in your wearable data," and her reply, "which wearable?" (an7u-tVP5Xc [28:44]).

**Related** — [[claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits]] (the reference measures). [[heuristic--survey-strengths-and-weaknesses-for-athlete-research]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] in the Old Bull library (combining independent evidence before acting).
=== heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match.md
---

# Plan Rest Over a Rolling Horizon, Not Just the Next Match

**What it is** — Two points from the talk. First, the greedy rule of picking the best team for each match ignores long-term injury and absence risk, and the presenters found real coaches' selections closer to the greedy model (82% similar) than to their search model (76%), which they attribute to short-term job pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43], [14:48]). Second, in the Q&A, a questioner (not named) compared it to an American "survivor pool" in which picking the best matchups early corners you later, and suggested optimizing only the next X games and re-optimizing as injuries occur and player skill estimates change (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49], [16:20]). The presenter replied that the model has a parameter for how many games forward to simulate, from the end of the season to a five-game window moved forward week by week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' stated reason is that rest taken now has a payoff in later matches, and a short window lets the coach re-plan with real information on who is available (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:20]). The presenter gives no result comparing a five-game window with a full-season horizon. Inference: a shorter horizon trades some foresight for robustness to model error, since injury and skill estimates drift.

**When to apply** — When planning rest or playing time across a congested stretch: set an explicit horizon (for example, the next several games), re-plan each week with updated availability, and name what the greedy option would be so the cost of the short-term choice is visible. Eric's baseline: in football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason the priority window (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Explicit), and bye weeks give players with few snaps harder practice (Q17, Explicit). Inference: those are horizon decisions already made by calendar, and the heuristic asks whether any are made match by match instead.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the horizon parameter is described, not evaluated, and the greedy-versus-search similarity numbers come from one league's open data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [10:12]). The explanation of coaches' choices (job pressure) is the presenters' belief. In football the roster and the game schedule give one game a week and no free rotation, so the "next X games" horizon is short already.

**Example** — The questioner's own analogy: a survivor-pool player who uses all the best teams early has nothing left late in the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].
=== principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it.md
---

# Asking About Menstrual Status Is Not the Same as Testing It

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari," a sports doctor and endocrinologist) makes a measurement-validity point: asking someone about their cycle is "not the same as actually testing the hormone levels" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Someone on a birth control pill who reports a period has a withdrawal bleed while taking exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). She asks researchers to use the same terminology: a withdrawal bleed from a pill, a naturally menstruating woman, and someone who ovulated and has a normal cycle are "all very different things" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:01] to [20:32]). On her audit's gold, silver and bronze classification, she says gold and silver are where studies did some hormonal measurement and also reported and asked about status (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00] to [19:30]); bronze is not defined in the transcript.

She also says it is not known whether training should change by cycle phase: "we don't know when it matters because we're not studying it enough," and it may be that nothing needs to change in someone without symptoms (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43] to [09:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the definitional reasons above and no data. Inference: grouping athletes by self-reported phase mixes people with different hormonal states, which would blur any phase comparison, but she does not run this through.

**When to apply** — Inference: before any internal analysis groups women athletes by cycle phase, record how status was determined (asked, hormone-tested, or on a pill with a withdrawal bleed). Athletic Medicine and Performance Nutrition would own the health data; Eric's baseline: Performance Nutrition is a separate unit that owns body composition and fueling (Explicit, Playbook p.5), and no force-plate or GPS data flow to it proactively (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q24). Inference: so who records cycle information and where it is stored would need agreeing between those units.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: these are definitions and an expert's position, with no data or citations in the talk. It gives no training recommendation by phase; she says the evidence is missing (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43]). It does not say how often hormone testing is needed or practical for a team. It is not a clinical guide for any individual.

**Example** — The speaker's own: an athlete says "I'm on my period" while taking a birth control pill; that is a withdrawal bleed on exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Inference: a study coding her as in a natural cycle phase would misclassify her.

**Related** — [[claim--audit-results-female-participation-and-menstrual-reporting]]. [[claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits]].
